publications.title: Who Holds the Pen? Preserving Clinicians' Role in Human-AI Interpretation for Child Language Therapy
publications.authors: Ko, K., Lim, C., Oh, M., Park, J., Oh, J., Kang, S., Gim, B., Kim, W., Kim, S.
publications.abstract: Child language therapy for developmental language disorder relies on clinicians' interpretive judgments, which directly shape children's developmental trajectories. As artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) are integrated into therapeutic workflows, questions arise regarding how to support interpretation without undermining professional agency and accountability. We examine this through a within-subjects study with eight Speech-Language Pathologists, comparing four human-AI collaboration modes that vary in AI autonomy and interaction structure. By situating these configurations within the domain of clinical interpretation, the study provides an empirical account of how different forms of AI assistance are experienced in practice. While greater autonomy reduced effort and increased perceived usefulness, it diminished clinicians' sense of control and professional identity. Despite comparable efficiency, participants consistently preferred a collaborative dialogue mode. These findings show that differences in adoption intention between AI-assisted configurations cannot be fully explained by perceived usefulness or effort reduction alone, but are associated with how interaction structures position clinicians within the interpretive process. They further suggest that, in contrast to more general-purpose domains, the use of AI in clinical interpretive work is shaped by the need to preserve authorship and professional agency. This study highlights the role of interaction structure in shaping professional experience and informs design principles for AI systems supporting clinical interpretation.
publications.thumbnailAlt: Clinician and AI jointly interpreting a child language therapy session, balancing agency and efficiency.
publications.summary: When AI helps interpret a child's language, clinicians still need to shape and take responsibility for that interpretation. In a study with eight speech-language pathologists, greater AI autonomy reduced effort but weakened perceived control and professional identity; participants preferred collaborative dialogue despite similar efficiency. The study suggests designing AI assistance around clinicians' participation in interpretation, preserving authorship alongside reducing workload.

publications.title: MagToTheFuture: Transforming Passive Objects into Circuit-Free Haptic Devices via Magnetic Fields
publications.authors: Park, J., Kang, S., Ko, K., Kim, G., Shin, S., Kang, Y., Matusik, W., Rus, D., Kim, S. J.
publications.journal: Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST 2026)
publications.thumbnailAlt: MagToTheFuture demonstration of magnetic-field haptic feedback through passive objects.
publications.summary: MagToTheFuture uses external magnetic fields to deliver force, vibration, and localized warmth through passive patches attached to everyday objects. Keeping the electronics in the surrounding platform enables multimodal haptic feedback without embedding powered actuators in each object, opening a path to augmenting ordinary artifacts while retaining their familiar physical form.

publications.title: PardonMix: Unpacking Ambiguity in Semantic Audio Mixing for Adaptive Interface Design
publications.authors: Kim, D., Ko, K., Oh, J., Kim, S.
publications.journal: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
publications.abstract: Audio mixing requires sophisticated parameter control and accumulated listening experience. In collaborative workflows, novice musicians often struggle to convey their auditory intent to professional engineers, creating a semantic gap between abstract descriptors and technical execution. While prior studies have mapped descriptive terms to parameters by focusing on minimizing ambiguity, we propose that identifying types of ambiguity can serve as a key to bridging this communication gap. We conducted a formative study analyzing mixing parameter vectors from 10 professional engineers for 18 abstract descriptors, identifying distinct types of ambiguity: High Consensus, Intensity Variance, and Directional Divergence. We propose PardonMix, an adaptive interface strategy that dynamically allocates disambiguation widgets; direct automation for high consensus terms, degree control for intensity varying terms, and exploratory gallery for divergent terms. PardonMix seeks to bridge the semantic gap by embracing ambiguity, facilitating smoother collaboration that ensures the novice’s artistic vision is precisely translated into technical execution.
publications.thumbnailAlt: PardonMix workflow from audio-mixing descriptors to three ambiguity categories and adaptive interface designs.
publications.summary: A study with 10 professional audio engineers found that ambiguous mixing terms differ in whether engineers agree on a setting, disagree on its strength, or interpret it in different directions. PardonMix maps these differences to automation, intensity controls, and exploratory alternatives. Its central design implication is that interfaces should adapt to the kind of ambiguity to better preserve musicians' intent.

publications.title: Demonstrating InteractiSense: An Interactive Tool for Supporting Social Engagement for Children with ASD
publications.authors: Kim, W.*, Lim, C.*, Seong, M., Ko, K., Kim, S.
publications.journal: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
publications.abstract: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are prone to disengagement during social activities, which limits opportunities for communication and peer interaction. We present InteractiSense, a spherical, sensing-integrated tangible prototype and cooperative serious game (SG) that targets social and collaborative scenarios for children with ASD. The prototype embeds seven sensors in a soft graspable body and streams multimodal data during play, while SG modules translate imitation, joint attention, and turn-taking objectives into shared gameplay. Prior to this demo, a preliminary study with 15 children with ASD has examined data stability and in-game experience. In this Interactive Demo, attendees experience InteractiSense through paired gameplay and a real-time visualization interface that exposes engagement-related signals. The demo aims to prompt discussion within the CHI community on inclusive SG content, tangible input mechanisms, and opportunities for physical AI systems in developmental contexts.
publications.thumbnailAlt: InteractiSense sensor-equipped handheld device and a turn-taking game for social engagement.
publications.summary: InteractiSense combines a soft, sensor-equipped object with cooperative games that turn imitation, joint attention, and turn-taking into shared play for children with ASD. It illustrates how tangible interaction and embedded sensing can bring social play and engagement-related observations into the same interface. A preliminary study with 15 children explored feasibility and play experience, without establishing therapeutic effectiveness.

publications.title: LEGOLAS: Learning & Enhancing Golf Skills through LLM-Augmented System
publications.authors: Ko, K., Oh, M., Seong, M., Kim, S.
publications.journal: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
publications.abstract: Abstract summary: This study examines how large language models and retrieval-augmented generation can provide verbal feedback for golf self-training. Unlike visual error displays alone, the feedback explains causes and possible corrections. The study reports improvements in learners' mental representations and continued skill development. Combining verbal and visual feedback supports learning efficiency and confidence in self-assessment without increasing cognitive load. The approach aims to make expert-informed feedback more accessible during independent practice.
publications.summary: Seeing a swing error does not necessarily tell a golfer why it happened or how to correct it. LEGOLAS combines visual feedback with LLM- and retrieval-based verbal guidance to make expert-informed explanations available during self-training. Reported improvements in learning efficiency and self-assessment confidence, without increased cognitive load, suggest that automated feedback should help learners understand corrections and judge their own practice, rather than only display deviations.
publications.thumbnailAlt: LEGOLAS golf-swing replay comparing target and user motion with LLM-generated verbal feedback.

publications.title: Leveraging voice for early detection of chronic kidney disease: Enabling continuous monitoring in remote healthcare
publications.authors: Ko, K., Ryu, J., Kim, S.
publications.abstract: Abstract summary: This paper explores voice-based machine learning as a non-invasive supplement to conventional chronic kidney disease assessment. It uses vocal changes associated with the condition as potential indicators and reports an F1 score of 0.86. The study discusses how this approach could support remote monitoring and telemedicine, alongside existing clinical tests.
publications.summary: Assessing kidney disease usually depends on clinical tests, which limits opportunities for low-burden remote assessment. This study examines whether voice features, combined with basic health information, can distinguish CKD stages 3–5 from healthy cases and stages 1–2. It explores making health-status information more accessible through a familiar input: speech. The results motivate further validation for remote severity assessment, not replacement of established tests or a claim of reliable long-term monitoring.

publications.title: A Survey on 3D Scene Graphs: Definition, Generation and Application
publications.authors: Bae, J.*, Shin, D.*, Ko, K., Lee, J., Kim, U.-H.
publications.abstract: Abstract summary: This survey reviews how 3D scene graphs represent objects, their properties, and relationships in an environment. It clarifies definitions, organizes advances in graph generation, examines applications, and identifies future directions for 3D scene understanding.
publications.summary: This survey organizes 3D scene graph research around definitions, generation methods, and applications, clarifying how objects, their properties, and their relationships can be represented together. It highlights the value of relational scene representations for intelligent agents: understanding how an environment is structured can support richer reasoning than recognizing individual objects alone.

projects.title: Soridam: Keeping Family Voices and Emotions Alive, Wherever You Are
projects.description: Family members living in different regions and time zones may miss the tone and everyday moments that make communication feel personal. Soridam combines photos and voice messages in a family-oriented social app, with emotion-recognition-based emoji previews and an archive for revisiting familiar voices. The project explores how voice can carry emotional context and preserve shared memories when family members cannot be together.

projects.title: Be With You: A Soft Hug for Every Silent Struggle
projects.description: Putting difficult feelings into words can be a barrier to reflecting on them. Be With You uses an LLM-based conversation guided by a psychological wellness framework to help users describe and organize their thoughts. Capybara characters and a personalized message of encouragement accompany the conversation. The project explores a gentle entry point to self-guided emotional reflection through conversation and affective feedback.

projects.title: Peach Seoga: Text Simplification Platform for Slow Learners
projects.description: Adapting everyday information into easy-to-read materials takes repeated work from educators and accessibility specialists. With the non-profit Peach Market, I helped develop an LLM-powered service that turns source content into accessible drafts for learners with cognitive or developmental challenges. Prompts were co-designed with experts, and users choose the output format. The service supports the drafting step so specialists can focus on reviewing and adapting materials to learners' needs.
